title: Ashura, remembered grief
hook: Shia Muslims mourn Husayn's death at Karbala; Sunni Muslims fast this day recalling Moses' rescue

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Good Friday, with its bare altars and silence. Your line was a quiet hour.

Two homes, the same morning. In the first, a family dresses in black. Tonight they'll go to a gathering where a reciter tells an old story, slowly, in a voice that breaks, and people in the room weep with him. In the second home, someone skips breakfast and lunch, fasting, and breaks the fast at sunset with dates and water. Both households are Muslim. Both are keeping the same day, the tenth of the month of Muharram. Its name is Ashura.
screen: `ONE FAMILY IN BLACK.` → `ANOTHER, FASTING TILL SUNSET.` → `THE SAME DAY: ASHURA.`

segments.voice: First, the rescue. A report in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari says that when the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to Medina, he found the Jews of the city fasting on this day. They told him it was the day God saved the Children of Israel from their enemy, and that Moses had fasted on it. The Prophet said Muslims had a claim on Moses too, and he fasted the day and told others to fast. So in Sunni tradition, Ashura is a day of fasting and thanks for Moses' rescue. Second, the grief. Shia tradition remembers Husayn, the son of Ali and Fatima, the Prophet's grandson. Tradition tells how he set out with his family and a small band of companions, refused to give his allegiance to the ruler Yazid, and was surrounded on the plain of Karbala, in what is now Iraq. The story says they were cut off from the river and suffered thirst. On Ashura, Husayn and those with him were killed. Third, remembered grief. In Shia communities the story is retold every year at gatherings called majalis. People weep, recite poems of lament, and walk in processions. The grief is kept on purpose. In Shia tradition, mourning Husayn is an act of loyalty to him, and his stand is remembered as a stand against injustice. Fourth, two remembrances, side by side. Sunni tradition also honors Husayn as the Prophet's grandson, and Shia tradition also tells of the rescue of Moses. The day holds both. Grief that is remembered on a set day, in company, doesn't fade into silence.
screen: `A FAST FOR MOSES' RESCUE.` · `HUSAYN AT KARBALA.` · `GRIEF KEPT ON PURPOSE.` · `ONE DAY, TWO REMEMBRANCES.` · then, large: `REMEMBERED GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing you learned about Karbala today, a small band of companions, a river cut off, a grandson who would not give his allegiance, and hold it gently, as you'd hold a name at a memorial. Then, if a grief of your own is there, let it come near without pushing it away or digging for it. Let it be remembered for a few breaths, in company with a much older grief.
Ashura: the tenth of Muharram, a fast for Moses' rescue, and the day Shia Muslims mourn Husayn at Karbala. Today's word.
Your line: remembered grief. One day can hold a rescue and a mourning at once. Day seven hundred fifty-one, done.

howItsDone: On Ashura, Shia Muslims gather at majalis to hear the story of Karbala retold, recite laments, and join processions in mourning for Husayn; Sunni Muslims fast the day, following the hadith about Moses' rescue, and some fast the day before as well.
